solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution for p14</summary>It is not difficult to see that the desired result will occur when  $2024$  and  $2025$  are in the same row but  $2023$  is in a different row from those two. The placement of the other  $2022$  numbers is irrelevant. 

First, note that there are a total of   $$ \binom{2025}{3} $$   ways to place the numbers  $2023, 2024, 2025.$ Let us place  $2024$  and  $2025$  first and then  $2023.$ There are   $$ 45\cdot\binom{45}{2} $$   ways to choose the row and then choose the exact placement of  $2024$  and  $2025$  and there are   $$ 44\cdot45 $$   ways to choose the placement of  $2023$  such that it is not in the same row as  $2024$  and  $2025.$ Hence, the desired probability is
\begin{align*}
\frac{45\cdot\binom{45}{2}\cdot44\cdot45}{\binom{2025}{3}} &= \frac{45\cdot45\cdot44\cdot44\cdot45\cdot3\cdot2}{2025\cdot2024\cdot2023\cdot2} 
&= \frac{22\cdot45\cdot3}{23\cdot2023}.
\end{align*}
Since the greatest common divisor of the numerator and denominator is  $1,$  the answer is   $$ 22\cdot45\cdot3=\boxed{2970}. $$    $\square$</details>

solution_md:

<details><summary>'Solution'</summary>\begin{align*}
3x+y &= 3x + \frac{y}{3} + \frac{y}{3} + \frac{y}{3}
&\geq 4\sqrt[4]{(3x)(\frac{y}{3})(\frac{y}{3})(\frac{y}{3})}
&=4\sqrt[4]{\frac{1}{9}*\frac{16}{9}}
&= \boxed{\frac{8}{3}}
\end{align*}

What is the area of the region covered by circles  $(A_1A_2O)$ ,  $(A_3A_4O)$ ,  $(A_5A_6O)$ ,  $(A_7A_8O)$ ,  $(A_9A_{10}O)$ , and  $(A_{11}A_{12}O)$ ? $(ABC)$  denotes the circle passing through points  $A,B$ , and  $C$ .**p20.** Let  $N = 2000... 0x0 ... 00023$  be a  $2023$ -digit number where the  $x$  is the  $23$ rd digit from the right. If $ N$  is divisible by  $13$ , compute  $x$ .**p21.** Alice and Bob each visit the dining hall to get a grilled cheese at a uniformly random time between  $12$  PM and  $1$  PM (their arrival times are independent) and, after arrival, will wait there for a uniformly random amount of time between  $0$  and  $30$  minutes. What is the probability that they will meet?

solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution for p20</summary>Let   $$ N' = 200\ldots0023, $$   where there are  $2020$  zeroes.

Note that   $$ N = N' + x\cdot10^{2000}. $$  Since
\begin{align*}
N' &= 2\cdot10^{2022} + 23 
&= 2\cdot(10^3)^{674} + 23 
&= 2\cdot(1000)^{674}+23 
&\equiv 2\cdot(-1)^{674}+10 
&\equiv 2\cdot1+10 
&\equiv 2+10 
&\equiv 12 \pmod{13},
\end{align*}
and
\begin{align*}
10^{2000} &= (10^3)^{666}\cdot100 
&= 1000^{666} \cdot 100 
&\equiv (-1)^{666}\cdot9 
&\equiv 1\cdot9 
&\equiv 9 \pmod{13},
\end{align*}
it follows that
\begin{align*}
N = N'+x\cdot10^{2000} &\implies N \equiv N'+x\cdot10^{2000} \pmod{13} 
&\implies 0 \equiv 12+9x \pmod{13} 
&\implies 9x \equiv 1 \pmod{13} 
&\implies x \equiv 3 \pmod{13} 
&\implies x=\boxed{3}.
\end{align*} $\square$</details>

stem_md: Let  $\triangle ABC$  be an equilateral triangle with side length  $6.$  Three circles of radius  $6$  are centered at  $A,$   $B,$  and  $C.$  Compute the radius of the circle that is centered at the center of  $\triangle ABC,$  is internally tangent to these three circles, and lies in the interior of the three circles.
solution_md:
<details><summary>sol</summary>[asy]
pair A=(0,0), B=(6,0), C=(3,3sqrt(3)),D=(3,sqrt(3)), E=(6-3sqrt(3),3);
draw(circle((0,0), 6));
draw(circle((6,0),6));
draw(circle((3,3sqrt(3)),6));
draw(circle(D, 6-2sqrt(3)));
draw(A--B--C--A);
draw(B--E);
label(" $A$ ", A, SW);
label(" $B$ ", B, SE);
label(" $C$ ", C, N);
label(" $O$ ", D, S);
label(" $E$ ", E, NW);
dot(D);
[/asy]
Let the center of  $\triangle ABC$  be  $O$  and let the point of tangency of the circle centered at  $O$  with the circle centered at  $B$  be  $E.$  Clearly,  $E,$   $O,$  and  $B$  are collinear, and since  $OB=\dfrac{2}{3}\cdot 3 \sqrt{3}=2\sqrt{3},$   $OE=BE-BO=\boxed{6-2\sqrt{3}}.$</details>

stem_md: Let  $\triangle OAB$  and  $\triangle OA^{\prime}B^{\prime}$  be equilateral triangles such that  $\angle AOA^{\prime}=90^{\circ},$   $\angle BOB^{\prime}=90^{\circ},$  and  $\angle AOB^{\prime}$  is obtuse. Given that the side length of  $\triangle OA^{\prime}B^{\prime}$  is  $1$  and the circumradius of  $\triangle OAB^{\prime}$  is  $\sqrt{61},$  compute the side length of  $\triangle AOB.$
solution_md:
<details><summary>sol</summary>Let  $AB=x\sqrt{3}.$  Note that  $\angle A^{\prime}OB=30^{\circ},$  so $\angle B^{\prime}OA=\angle B^{\prime}OA^{\prime}+\angle A^{\prime}OA+\angle BOA=60^{\circ}+30^{\circ}+60^{\circ}=150^{\circ}.$  By the law of cosines,  $B^{\prime}A=\sqrt{B^{\prime}O^2+OA^2-2\cdot B^{\prime}O\cdot OA\cdot \cos(150^{\circ})}=\sqrt{1+3x^2-2\cdot x\sqrt{3}\cdot\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)}=\sqrt{3x^2+3x+1}.$  Then,  $\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot B^{\prime}O\cdot OA\cdot \sin(150^{\circ})=\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot x\sqrt{3}\cdot \dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{x\sqrt{3}}{4}=[B^{\prime}OA]=\dfrac{B^{\prime}O\cdot OA\cdot B^{\prime} A}{4\sqrt{61}}=\dfrac{x\sqrt{3}\sqrt{3x^2+3x+1}}{4\sqrt{61}}.$  Thus,  $\sqrt{3x^2+3x+1}=\sqrt{61},$  so  $3x^2+3x+1-61=3x^2+3x-60=3(x^2+x-20)=3(x+5)(x-4)=0,$  so  $x=-5$  or  $x=4.$  Clearly,  $x\neq -5,$  so  $x=4$  and  $AB=x\sqrt{3}=\boxed{4\sqrt{3}}.$ [asy]
pair B=(0,0), A=(4sqrt(3),0), O=(2sqrt(3),6);
pair D=(3sqrt(3)/2, 13/2), C=(3sqrt(3)/2, 11/2);
draw(O--A--B--O--D--C--O--D--A);
dot(D);
dot(C);
dot(O);
dot(A);
dot(B);
label(" $A$ ", A, SE);
label(" $B$ ", B, SW);
label(" $O$ ", O, NE);
label(" $B^{\prime}$ ", D, NW);
label(" $A^{\prime}$ ", C, SW);
[/asy]</details>

stem_md: In right triangle  $\vartriangle ABC$  with right angle at  $B$ , let  $I$  be the incenter and  $G$  the centroid. Let the foot of the perpendicular from  $I$  to  $AB$  be  $D$  and the foot of the perpendicular from  $G$  to  $CB$  be  $E$ . Line  $\ell$  is drawn such that  $\ell$  is parallel to  $DE$  and passes through  $B$ . Line  $ID$  meets  $\ell$  at  $X$ , and line GE meets  $\ell$  at  $Y$  . Given that  $AB=8$  and  $CB= 15$ , compute the length  $XY$  .
solution_md:
<details><summary>sol</summary>[asy]
pair B=(0,0), A=(0,8), C=(15,0), I=(3,3), D=(0,3), H=(3,0), Z=(75/17, 96/17);
draw(A--B--C--cycle);
label(" $A$ ", A, N);
label(" $B$ ", B, SW);
label(" $C$ ", C, SE);
label(" $I$ ", I, NW);
draw(circle(I, 3));
dot(I);
draw(I--D--I--H--I--Z);
label(" $D$ ", D, W);
label(" $H$ ", H, S);
label(" $Z$ ", Z, NE);
[/asy]

We set up a coordinate plane with  $B=(0,0),$   $C=(15,0),$  and  $A=(0,8).$  Let  $H$  and  $Z$  be the feet of the altitudes from  $I$  to  $BC$  and  $AC,$  respectively. Then, observe that  $BDIH$  is a square, so if  $r$  is the inradius,  $BD=DI=IH=BH=r.$  Now, by equal tangents,  $AD=AZ=8-r$  and  $CH=CZ=15-r.$  By the Pythagorean Theorem,  $17=AC=AZ+CZ=23-2r,$  so  $r=3.$  Now,  $I=(3,3).$ Observe that the centroid is just the average of the coordinates for  $A,$   $B,$  and  $C,$  which is  $G=\left(5, \dfrac{8}{3}\right),$  so  $E=(5,0).$  Also,  $D=(0,3),$  so the slope of line  $DE$  is  $-\dfrac{3}{5}$  and thus line  $l$  has equation  $y=-\dfrac{3x}{5}.$  Also, line  $ID$  has equation  $y=3,$  so  $X=(-5,3),$  and line  $GE$  has equation  $x=5,$  so  $Y=(5,-3).$  Now,  $XY=\sqrt{(-5-5)^2+(3-(-3))^2}=\sqrt{136}=\boxed{2\sqrt{34}}.$</details>

stem_md: Consider the horizontal line that intersects the ellipse  $\frac{x^2}{9}+y^2=1$  at points  $A$  and  $B$  above the  $x$ - axis such that  $\angle AOB = 120^o$ ,  where point  $O$  is the origin. Compute the area of the region of the ellipse that lies above this line.
solution_md:
If  $\angle{AOB}= \frac{2\pi}{3}$ , then taking the lines  $y = \pm \tan(\pi/6)x = \pm \frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}$  intersected with the ellipse yields: $\frac{x^2}{9}+\frac{x^2}{3}=1 \Rightarrow x = \pm \frac{3}{2} \Rightarrow y = \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\left(\frac{3}{2}\right) = \left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right) =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ .

The area in question computes to: $A = \int_{-3/2}^{3/2} \sqrt{1-\frac{x^2}{9}} - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} dx= \textcolor{red}{\frac{2\pi-3\sqrt{3}}{4}}$ .

**p1.** Viktor wants to build a big sandcastle with a triangle base. What is the maximum area of a right triangle with hypotenuse  $10$ ?**p2.** For his  $21$ st birthday, Arpit would like to play a game of  $21$ . He would like to achieve  $21$  total points by drawing three cards and adding up their point values, with the third card’s point value being worth twice as much (multiplied by two in the sum). If there are infinite cards with point values  $1$  through  $14$ , how many ways are there for him to get to  $21$ ? Note that the order of the cards drawn matters.**p3.** Compute the number of positive integers  $n$  less than  $100$  such that  $n^2$  divides  $n!$ .


PS. You should use hide for answers. Collected [here](https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c5h2760506p24143309).
solution_md: <details><summary>P1</summary>The maximum area of a right triangle with hypotenuse  $10$  is simply the area of a right isosceles triangle with hypotenuse  $10$ , so the leg of the triangle is  $\frac{10}{\sqrt{2}}$ , so the answer is  $\frac{\left(\frac{10}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2}{2}=\frac{\frac{100}{2}}{2}=\boxed{25}$ .</details>

In case  $n>p^2$  we have  $2\leq p < \frac{n}{p}< n$  and therefore  $\left(p\cdot \frac{n}{p}\right)\mid (n-1)!$ .

In case  $n=p^2$  with  $p>2$  we have  $2\leq p < \frac{2n}{p}< n$  and therefore  $\left(p\cdot \frac{2n}{p}\right)\mid (n-1)!$ .

It remains case  $n=4$ , where 4 not divides  $3!=6$ . There are 25 primes below 100, so the answer is  $99-25-1 = \fbox{73}$ .</details>

**p13.** Compute the remainder when  $(10!)^{20}$  is divided by  $2024$ .**p14.** A right square pyramid with height  $12$  and a base of side length  $10$  is inscribed in sphere  $S$ . Compute the largest possible radius of a sphere that lies inside  $S$  and is tangent to one of the lateral faces of the pyramid.**p15.** For any integer  $n \ge 2$ , with prime factorization  $n= p^{a_1}_1p^{a_2}_2 ... p^{a_k}_k$ , we let  $f(n) = \sum^k_{i=1} p_ia_i$ . For example, since  $90 = 2^1\cdot 3^2 \cdot  5^1$ , we have  $f(90) = 2 \cdot 1 + 3 \cdot 2 + 5 \cdot 1 = 13$ . Let  $m$  be the minimum value that  $f(n)$  can take on for all integers  $n > 2024$ . Find the smallest integer   $k \ge 2$  such that  $f(k)=m$ .


PS. You should use hide for answers. Collected [here](https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c5h2760506p24143309).
solution_md:
Solution for p13Let $N=(10!)^{20}.$ Firstly, it is obvious that $N \equiv 0 \pmod{8}.$ Then, by Wilson's Theorem, we have \begin{align*} N &\equiv (-1)^{20} &\equiv 1 \pmod{11}. \end{align*} Finally, expanding out $10!$ and reducing it modulo $23,$ we get $21,$ so Fermat's Little Theorem tells us that \begin{align*} N &\equiv 21^{20} &\equiv (-2)^{-2} &\equiv \frac{1}{4} &\equiv 6 \pmod{23}. \end{align*} Finally, by the Chinese Remainder Theorem, the answer is $N \equiv \boxed{144} \pmod{2024}.$ $\square$
Solution for p14Firstly, by the Pythagorean Theorem, we have $$ (12-r)^2+(5\sqrt{2})^2=r^2 \implies r = \frac{97}{12}. $$ Now, we also know that the height from the apex of any of the lateral faces is $$ \sqrt{12^2+5^2}=13, $$ so it follows by similar triangles that the distance from the center of $S$ to any of the lateral faces is $$ \frac{\tfrac{97}{12}}{13} \cdot 5 = \frac{97}{12} \cdot \frac{5}{13}. $$ It results that the radius of the largest sphere that is tangent to one of the lateral faces of the pyramid is \begin{align*} \frac{\tfrac{97}{12} \cdot \tfrac{5}{13} + \tfrac{97}{12}}{2} &= \frac{97}{12} \cdot \frac{18}{13} \cdot \frac{1}{2} &= \boxed{\frac{291}{52}}. \end{align*} $\square$
Solution for p15By Bertrand's Postulate, for all primes $p \ge 5,$ there exists a prime $q$ less than $p$ such that $2p>q.$ Also, we know that $q+2 \le p$ for these primes, so it follows that as long as some prime greater than $3$ divides $n,$ there exists some $m \ge n$ such that $f(m) \le f(n).$ Hence, suppose that only $2$ and $3$ divide $n.$ Then, taking casework on whether $\nu_2(n)=0, 1, \ldots, 10$ and finding the least possible value of $\nu_3(n)$ such that $2^{\nu_2(n)}3^{\nu_3(n)}>2024,$ we find that the smallest possible value of $2\nu_2(n)+3\nu_3(n)$ among all of the pairs we derive is $21,$ achieved by $(\nu_2(n), \nu_3(n))=(0, 7).$ Now, we wish to find the smallest integer $k \ge 2$ such that $f(k)=21.$ I will prove the following lemma:**Claim:** If $2 \mid k,$ then the two smallest odd primes that can divide $k$ are $7$ and $13.$ *Proof.* It suffices to show that $3, 5,$ and $11$ cannot divide $k.$ All of these primes are the smaller prime in a twin prime pair, so it suffices to show that a prime $p$ cannot divide $k$ if $p+2$ is also prime. Suppose for the sake of contradiction that $2 \mid k, p \mid k,$ and $p+2$ is prime for a prime $p.$ Then, we clearly have $p+2<2p,$ so the positive integer $$ k'=\frac{k(p+2)}{2p} $$ is smaller than $k$ and satisfies $f(k')=f(k),$ contradicting the minimality of $k.$ $\blacksquare$ Hence, it follows that the only positive integers the even $k$ case gives are $2^7 \cdot 7=896$ and $2^4 \cdot 13=208.$ Otherwise, $k$ is odd, so simply need to consider the primes $3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17,$ and $19.$ Furthermore, at least three of them (including repeats) must be in the prime factorization of $k,$ so $17$ and $19$ are ruled out. Now, it is not difficult to deduce via casework on the number of primes (including repeats) that divide $k$ that the possible multisets of primes that divide $k$ are: $$ \{3,5, 13\}, \{3, 7, 11\}, \{5, 5, 11\}, \{3, 3, 3, 5, 7\}, \{3,3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3\}. $$ These give the numbers $195, 231, 275, 945,$ and $2187,$ so the final answer is $$ \min(896, 208, 195, 231, 275, 945, 2187)=\boxed{195}. $$ $\square$

solution_md: <details><summary>P16</summary>Notice that since  $\text{gcd}(2023,4202) = 1,$   $2023$  is primitive  $\mod 4202.$  In particular, as  $k$  runs from  $1$  to  $4201,$   $2023k$  runs across each nonzero residue  $\mod 4202$  exactly once. <details><summary>p7</summary>Let  $L = \lim_{t\to 0}\left(\prod_{n=2}^{\infty}\left(1+\frac{t}{n(n+1)}\right)\right)^{\frac{1}{t}}$ .
Taking the natural logs of both sides gives
\[
\ln L = \frac{1}{t}\sum_{n=2}^{\infty} \ln\!\left(1+\frac{t}{n(n+1)}\right).
\]
Define  $f(t)=\frac{1}{t}\ln\left(1+\frac{t}{n(n+1)}\right)$ , and  $g(n)=\frac{1}{n(n+1)}.$ Then for fixed  $n$ ,
\[
\lim_{t\to 0} f(t) = \lim_{t\to 0} \frac{\ln(1+t a_n)}{t} = a_n.
\]

Fix  $|t|<\frac{1}{2}$ , since  $|t a_n|\le \frac{1}{8}$ , we have
\[
|f(t)| = \left|\frac{\ln(1+t a_n)}{t}\right| \le \frac{a_n}{1-\frac{1}{8}} = \frac{8}{7}a_n.
\]
By the Dominated Convergence Theorem,
\[
\ln L = \sum_{n=2}^{\infty} \lim_{t\to 0} f(t) = \sum_{n=2}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n(n+1)}.
\]
Tele tele telescoping gives
\[
\sum_{n=2}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n(n+1)} = \sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\left(\frac{1}{n}-\frac{1}{n+1}\right) = \frac{1}{2}.
\]
So we have  $L = e^{\frac{1}{2}} = \boxed{\sqrt{e}}$ .</details>

solution_md: P23 sillied this question on the test<details><summary>sol</summary>Let's count the numbers that aren't in the range of the function. First off, let us notice when this function jumps from one value to the next. Clearly this is when a number  $n-1$  approaches  $n$  jumps to when the number is exactly  $n$  and then to when  $n$  goes to  $n+1$ . From here, we can write it numerically as  $n(2n-1)$  to  $2n^2$  to  $n(2n+1)$ . Note that 2n^2 is in the range of the function, so we exclude this. From here it just becomes  $ [n(2n-1),2n^2)\cup(2n^2,n(2n+1)]$ , which totals up to  $2n$  integers that aren't in the range in each gap. Next, we want to find the maximum. Notice that when an integer is between  $31$  and  $32$ , it works, and  $32$  to  $33$  doesn't. This means that  $31$  is the maximum number which we can get a gap. Notice that if  $n$  is  $32$ , we get a gap of  $10$  integers since  $2025$  is the maximum number we can go to. From here, we can calculate our final answer.   $$ 10+\sum_{n=1}^{n=31}2n=10+992=\boxed{1002} $$</details>

\mathrm a. ~ 6/7\qquad \mathrm b.~5/7\qquad \mathrm c. ~1/2 \qquad \mathrm d. ~4/5 \qquad \mathrm e. ~3/5
\]
solution_md:
From  $B$ , draw a cevian that  $BD$  such that  $BDC$  is isosceles. Then, it must follow that  $ABD$  is a right triangle. Let  $BD = DC = x$ .
Then  $AD = 2-x$ . Since  $ABD$  is right, applying Pythagorean Theorem gives that  $x = \frac{3}{4}$ . Thus,  $\sin A = \frac{3}{5}$ . Then
\[ [ABC] = \frac{AB \cdot AC \cdot \sin A}{2} = \frac{1\cdot 2 \cdot \frac{3}{5}}{2} = \frac{3}{5} \] 
so the answer is (E).

We have\begin{align*}\cos \angle ACB & =\frac{\cos \angle ACB}{\sin \angle ACB}\sin \angle ACB & =\frac{\sin (90^\circ +\angle ACB)}{\sin \angle ACB}\sin \angle ACB & =\frac{\sin \angle ABC}{\sin \angle ACB}\sin \angle ACB & =\frac{AC}{AB}\sin \angle ACB & =\frac{2}{1}\sin \angle ACB & =2\sin \angle ACB, \end{align*}hence $\cos ^2\angle ACB=4\sin ^2\angle ACB=4-4\cos ^2\angle ACB$ , which gives $\cos ^2\angle ACB=\frac{4}{5}$ , and therefore $\sin ^2\angle ACB=\frac{1}{5}$ . Then\begin{align*}\sin \angle BAC & =\sin (\angle ABC+\angle ACB) & =\sin (90^\circ +\angle ACB+\angle ACB) & =\sin (90^\circ +2\angle ACB) & =\cos (2\angle ACB) & =\cos ^2\angle ACB-\sin ^2\angle ACB & =\frac{4}{5}-\frac{1}{5} & =\frac{3}{5}. \end{align*}Hence\begin{align*}[ABC] & =\frac{BA\cdot AC\cdot \sin \angle BAC}{2} & =\frac{1\cdot 2\cdot \sin \angle BAC}{2} & =\sin \angle BAC & =\frac{3}{5}. \end{align*}

\mathrm a. ~ 15^\circ\qquad \mathrm b.~30^\circ \qquad \mathrm c. ~45^\circ \qquad \mathrm d. ~60^\circ \qquad \mathrm e. ~90^\circ\]

stem_md: Let  $a, b, c, d, e$  be real numbers such that  $a<b<c<d<e.$  The least possible value of the function  $f: \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$  with  $f(x) = |x-a| + |x - b|+ |x - c| + |x - d|+ |x - e|$  is  $$ \mathrm a. ~ e+d+c+b+a\qquad \mathrm b.~e+d+c-b-a\qquad \mathrm c. ~e+d+|c|-b-a \qquad \mathrm d. ~e+d+b-a \qquad \mathrm e. ~e+d-b-a $$
solution_md: Let $a, b, c, d, e$ be real numbers such that $a Over $(-\infty,a)$ , $f(x)=(a+b+c+d+e)-5x$ Over $[a,b)$ , $f(x)=(-a+b+c+d+e)-3x$ Over $[b,c)$ , $f(x)=(-a-b+c+d+e)-x$ Over $[c,d)$ , $f(x)=(-a-b-c+d+e)+x$ Over $[d,e)$ , $f(x)=(-a-b-c-d+e)+3x$ Over $[e,+\infty)$ , $f(x)=(-a-b-c-d-e)+5x$ So $f(x)$ is continuous, decreasing over $(-\infty,c]$ and increasing over $[c,+\infty)$ and so its minimum is $\boxed{f(c)=-a-b+d+e}$ (solution e) (note that depending on values of $a,b,c,d,e$ , other solutions are possible ;) but solution e is the only true whatever are $a,b,c,d,e$ matching the problem statement)

solution_md:
A sequence $a_1, a_2, \ldots$ satisfies $a_1 = \dfrac 52$ and $a_{n + 1} = {a_n}^2 - 2$ for all $n \ge 1.$ Let $M$ be the integer which is closest to $a_{2023}.$ The last digit of $M$ equals $$ \mathrm a. ~ 0\qquad \mathrm b.~2\qquad \mathrm c. ~4 \qquad \mathrm d. ~6 \qquad \mathrm e. ~8 $$
Immediate to get $a_n=u_n+\frac 1{u_n}$ with $u_1=2$ and $u_{n+1}=u_n^2$ So $a_{2023}=2^{2^{2023}}+2^{-2^{2023}}$ So $M=2^{2^{2023}}$ and since we have $2^{4n}\equiv 6\pmod{10}$ $\forall n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$ , Answer is $\boxed 6$

stem_md: How many ordered triples of integers  $(a, b, c)$  satisfy the following system?  $$ \begin{cases} ab + c &= 17  a + bc &= 19 \end{cases} $$    $$ \mathrm a. ~ 2\qquad \mathrm b.~3\qquad \mathrm c. ~4 \qquad \mathrm d. ~5 \qquad \mathrm e. ~6 $$
solution_md:
Subtracting the equations gives  $(c-a) (b-1) = 2$ , so  $b \in \{-1,0,2,3\}$ , but  $b = -1$  clearly fails. So  $b \in \{0,2,3\}$ . 

Note that for a fixed value of  $b$  not equal to  $-1$  or  $1$ , there is at most one integer solution to the system, so we just need to find the number of  $b$  that yield a solution. 

If  $b = 0$ , take  $c = 17, a = 19$ . 

If  $b = 2$ , take  $a = 5, c = 7$ . 

If  $b  = 3$ , take  $a = 4, c = 5$ . 

So the answer is  $\boxed{ \mathrm b.~3} $ .

stem_md: Three positive real numbers  $a, b, c$  satisfy  $a^b = 343, b^c = 10, a^c = 7.$  Find  $b^b.$   $$ \mathrm a. ~ 1000\qquad \mathrm b.~900\qquad \mathrm c. ~1200 \qquad \mathrm d. ~4000 \qquad \mathrm e. ~100 $$
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>We have  $a=343^{1/b}=\left(7^3\right)^{1/b}=7^{3/b}$  and  $a=7^{1/c}.$  Thus,  $7^{3/b}=7^{1/c}\iff\frac3b=\frac1c\iff b=3c.$  Cubing the equation  $b^c=10$  gives  $b^b=b^{3c}=\boxed{\mathrm a.~1000}.$</details>

What is the least positive integer  $m$  such that the following is true?

*Given  $\it m$  integers between  $\it1$  and  $\it{2023},$  inclusive, there must exist two of them  $\it a, b$  such that  $1 < \frac ab \le 2.$* \[\mathrm a. ~ 10\qquad \mathrm b.~11\qquad \mathrm c. ~12 \qquad \mathrm d. ~13 \qquad \mathrm e. ~1415\]
solution_md: I got  $\boxed{12}$  as in my <details><summary>sol</summary>We want to construct a sequence such that  $a_i > 2a_{i-1}$  and then take one more than the number of terms to find the least  $m$  we need. We could start at  $1$  and do  $2a_i + 1$  but to maximize the terms we work backwards. Note that operating  $a_i = \lceil \frac{a_{i+1}}{2} \rceil - 1$  will ensure  $a_{i+1}$  is the least integer greater than  $2a_i$ . We start at  $2023$  and work backwards to  $2$  over 10 of these divisions, so we have  $m = 11 + 1 = \boxed{12}$ .</details>

Consider the quadratic equation   $$ (m + 1)x^2 + 4mx + m - 3 =0. $$  Which of the following must be true? $\quad\rm(I)$  Both roots of this equation must be real. $\quad\rm(II)$  If both roots are real, then one of the roots must be less than  $-1.$  $\quad\rm(III)$  If both roots are real, then one of the roots must be larger than  $1.$   $$ \mathrm a. ~ \text{Only} ~(\mathrm I)\rm \qquad \mathrm b. ~(I)~and~(II)\qquad \mathrm c. ~Only~(III) \qquad \mathrm d. ~Both~(I)~and~(III) \qquad \mathrm e. ~(I), (II),~and~(III) $$
solution_md:
Let $m \neq -1$ be a real number. Consider the quadratic equation $$ (m + 1)x^2 + 4mx + m - 3 =0. $$ Which of the following must be true? $\quad\rm(I)$ Both roots of this equation must be real. $\quad\rm(II)$ If both roots are real, then one of the roots must be less than $-1.$ $\quad\rm(III)$ If both roots are real, then one of the roots must be larger than $1.$ $$ \mathrm a. ~ \text{Only} ~(\mathrm I)\rm \qquad \mathrm b. ~(I)~and~(II)\qquad \mathrm c. ~Only~(III) \qquad \mathrm d. ~Both~(I)~and~(III) \qquad \mathrm e. ~(I), (II),~and~(III) $$
Discriminant is $12m^2+8m+12>0$ $\forall m$ and so always two distinct real roots $P(-1)=-2(m+1)$ has opposite sign to leading coefficient and so $-1$ is between the two roots and so exactly one root is less than $-1$ When $m=3$ , roots are $\{-3,0\}$ , none of which is $>1$ Hence $\boxed{(I)\text{ and }(II)}$

There are  $100$  people in a room. Some are *wise* and some are *optimists*. $\quad \bullet~$  A *wise* person can look at someone and know if they are wise or if they are an optimist. $\quad \bullet~$  An *optimist* thinks everyone is wise (including themselves).

Everyone in the room writes down what they think is the number of wise people in the room. What is the smallest possible value for the average?  $$ \mathrm a. ~ 10\qquad \mathrm b.~25\qquad \mathrm c. ~50 \qquad \mathrm d. ~75 \qquad \mathrm e. ~100 $$
solution_md:
There are $100$ people in a room. Some are *wise* and some are *optimists*. $\quad \bullet~$ A *wise* person can look at someone and know if they are wise or if they are an optimist. $\quad \bullet~$ An *optimist* thinks everyone is wise (including themselves). Everyone in the room writes down what they think is the number of wise people in the room. What is the smallest possible value for the average? $$ \mathrm a. ~ 10\qquad \mathrm b.~25\qquad \mathrm c. ~50 \qquad \mathrm d. ~75 \qquad \mathrm e. ~100 $$
$ x$ wise write $ x$ while $100-x$ optimist write $100$ and so average is $\frac{x^2+100(100-x)}{100}=75+\frac{(x-50)^2}{100}$ , whose minimum is $\boxed{75}$

stem_md:
Let  $0 \le a_1 \le a_2 \le \dots \le a_n \le 1$  be  $n$  real numbers with  $n \ge 2$ . Assume  $a_1 + a_2 + \dots + a_n \ge n-1$ . Prove that
\[ a_2a_3\dots a_n \ge \left( 1 - \frac 1n \right)^{n-1} \]
solution_md:
First, we may scale  $a_i$  by  $r<1$ , so that  $a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n = n-1$ . This scales the left hand side by  $r^{n-1}<1$ , so it is enough to prove the inequality assuming   $a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n = n-1$ .

Now, fix  $a_1 = a$ , and vary  $a_i$  for  $i \ge 2$  according to the conditions given. We do the following procedure on  $a_i$ : 
Initially, take  $p = 2$  and  $q = n$ . Also, assume that  $a_{n+1} = 1$ .
1. If  $p=q$ , then stop.
2. If  $|a_p - a_{p-1}| \ge |a_q - a_{q+1}|$ , then set  $a_q = a_{q+1}$ , decrease  $a_p$  by  $|a_q - a_{q+1}|$  and decrease  $q$  by  $1$ . Go to Step 1.
3. If  $|a_p - a_{p-1}| < |a_q - a_{q+1}|$ , then set  $a_p = a_{p-1}$ , increase  $a_q$  by  $|a_p - a_{p-1}|$  and increase  $p$  by  $1$ . Go to Step 1.

At every step the weakly increasing nature of  $a_i$  is preserved, as well as the sum of  $a_i$  is also preserved. Also, the product  $a_2 a_3\cdots a_n$  decreases at every step (since  $ab > (a-t)(b+t)$  if  $a<b$ ). Finally, the algorithm stops since  $|p-q|$  decreases by  $1$  at every step.

At the end of this process, every  $a_i$  except possibly one of them is equal to either  $a$  or  $1$ . Suppose  $a_1 = \cdots = a_k = a$ ,  $a_{k+1} = b$ ,  $a_{k+2} = \cdots = a_n = 1$ . Note also that the sequence  $ \left(1 - \frac 1n \right)^{n-1}$  is a strictly decreasing sequence. 

So, it suffices to prove that if  $k \cdot a + b = k$ , and  $0 \le a \le b \le 1$ , then  $\displaystyle a^{k-1}b \ge \left(1 - \frac{1}{k+1} \right)^k$ .

This can be dealt with by noting that  $a \le b$  implies that  $a \le \frac{k}{k+1}$  and  $b \le 1$  implies that  $\frac{k-1}{k} \le a$ . 
Now,  $a^{k-1}b = a^{k-1}(k - ka)$ , so it suffices to prove that  $f(a) = a^{k-1}(1-a)$  achieves its minimum in the interval  $\left[ \frac{k-1}{k}, \frac{k}{k+1} \right] $  at the point  $a = \frac{k}{k+1}$ . 
This is clear because  $f'(a) = a^{k-2}((k-1) - ka) \le 0$  in this interval, so it achieves the minimum when  $a$  is maximum, i.e. at  $a = \frac{k}{k+1}$ .  $\square$
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/USA Contests/USA - College-Hosted Events/UMD Math Competition/2023 UMD Math Competition Part II/3207528.json

stem_md:
Let  $p$  be a prime, and  $n > p$  be an integer. Prove that 
\[ \binom{n+p-1}{p} - \binom{n}{p} \] 
is divisible by  $n$ .
solution_md:
We begin with the observation that   $$ a_n = \binom{n+p-1}{p} - \binom{n}{p} = \frac np \left( \binom{n+p-1}{p-1} - \binom{n-1}{p-1} \right)  $$   Thus if  $(n,p) = 1$ , then  $n \mid a_n$ .

So, assume that  $p \mid n$ . Then it is enough to prove that   $$ p \mid \binom{n+p-1}{p-1} - \binom{n-1}{p-1} $$   but this is clear because  $(n+p-1) \cdot (n+p-2) \cdots (n+1) \equiv (n-1) \cdot (n-2) \cdots (n-p+1) \pmod p$ .

stem_md:
For how many pairs of integers  $(m, n)$  with  $0 < m \le n \le 50$  do there exist precisely four triples of integers  $(x, y, z)$  satisfying the following system?
\[\begin{cases} x^2 + y+ z = m  x + y^2 + z = n\end{cases}\]
\[\rm a. ~180\qquad \mathrm b. ~182\qquad \mathrm c. ~186 \qquad\mathrm d. ~188\qquad\mathrm e. ~190\]
solution_md:
For a 4-tuple  $(x,y,m,n)$  results an unique value of  $z$ .
Subtracting the equations results: $(y-x)(x+y-1)=n-m$ . $y-x$  and  $x+y-1$  have different parities, hence  $d=n-m$  is an even number.
For an even number  $d$  exist an unique pair of natural numbers  $(u,v)$ , where  $v$  is an odd number, such that  $d=2^u\cdot v$ .
For  $v=1$ , there are exactly  $4$  solutions  $(x,y)$  of the equation  $(y-x)(x+y-1)=n-m$ , respectively the solutions of the systems: $\begin{cases}y-x=2^ux+y-1=1\end{cases}\;\begin{cases}y-x=1 x+y-1=2^u\end{cases}\;\begin{cases}y-x=-2^ux+y-1=-1\end{cases}\;\begin{cases}y-x=-1 x+y-1=-2^u\end{cases}$ For  $v\ge3$ , in the systems can appear as odd numbers  $1$  and  $v$ , hence at least  $8$  distinct systems.

Results:  $d=n-m=2^u,\;u\in\mathbb{N}$ .
For a fixed  $d$  exist  $50-d$  pairs  $(m,n)\in\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N},\;0<m\le n\le50$  for which  $n-m=d$ , respectively  $(1,d+1),(2,d+2),...,(50-d,50)$ . $d=n-m\le 50-1=49\Longrightarrow d\in\{2,4,8,16,32\}\Longrightarrow 50-d\in\{48,46,42,34,18\}$ .

Results the number of triplets  $(x,y,z)$  satisfying the given conditions: $N_t=48+46+42+34+18=188$ .

stem_md: An equilateral triangle  $T$  and a circle  $C$  are on the same plane. Suppose each side length of  $T$  is  $6\sqrt3$  and the radius of  $C$  is  $2.$  The distance between the centers of  $T$  and  $C$  is  $15.$  For every two points  $X$  on  $T$  and  $Y$  on  $C,$  let  $M(X, Y)$  be the midpoint of segment  $\overline{XY}.$  The points  $M(X, Y)$  as  $X$  varies on  $T$  and  $Y$  varies on  $C$  create a region whose area is  $A.$  Find  $A.$ \[\mathrm a. ~\pi + 14\sqrt3 \qquad \mathrm b. ~3\pi + 10\sqrt3 \qquad \mathrm c. ~4\pi+9\sqrt3 \qquad\mathrm d. ~\pi + 15\sqrt3 \qquad\mathrm e. ~4\pi+6\sqrt3\]
solution_md:
Ah, if you specify that  $X$  and  $Y$  lie on the perimeter of  $T$  and  $C$ , then you do get an answer. Fix  $Y$  and vary  $X$ ; by homothety,  $M(X,Y)$  traces out an equilateral triangle with side length  $3\sqrt3$ . Fix  $X$  and vary  $Y$ ; by the same homothety,  $M(X,Y)$  traces out a circle with radius 1. Combining both moving points reveals that  $A$  is the locus of points within 1 from the perimeter of an equilateral triangle with side length  $3\sqrt3$ .

We can break this part up into four parts: 3 circular sectors with 120 degrees and radius 1, 3 rectangles with side lengths 1 and  $3\sqrt3$ , an equilateral triangle with side length  $3\sqrt3$ , and an equilateral triangle inside the first one. Notice that the first triangle has altitude  $9/2$  and the altitude of the second triangle is shortened by 1 on one side and 2 on another, for an altitude of  $3/2$ . Hence the second triangle has side length  $\sqrt{3}$ . The answer is
\[\pi+3(1)(3\sqrt3)+\frac{27\sqrt{3}}{4}-\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}=\pi+15\sqrt3\Longrightarrow\boxed{d}\]

stem_md: The width of a lane in a circular running track is  $1.22$  meters. One loop in the first lane (shortest lane) is  $400$  meters. Thus  $12.5$  loops makes it a  $5{,}000$  meter distance. Which lane should an athlete run in if they want to make  $12$  loops as close to the  $5{,}000$  meter distance as possible? \[\rm a. ~second\qquad \mathrm b. ~third \qquad \mathrm c. ~fourth \qquad\mathrm d. ~fifth \qquad\mathrm e. ~sixth\]
solution_md:
Let  $x$  be the extra distance so that 12 loops makes 5000 meters. This information can be written as
\[2\pi(12)\left(\frac{200}{\pi}+x\right)=5000\]
Solving, we find  $x\approx 2.65$ , which is about 2 lanes over. Thus we want the third lane, which is  $\boxed{b}$ .

stem_md:
For how many angles  $x$ , in radians, satisfying  $0\le x<2\pi$  do we have  $\sin(14x)=\cos(68x)$ ?
\[\rm a. ~128\qquad \mathrm b. ~130\qquad \mathrm c. ~132 \qquad\mathrm d. ~134\qquad\mathrm e. ~136\]
solution_md:
Solved with @idksomething, verified with Desmos counting.
The given equation is equivalent to  $\sin(14x)=\sin(\pi/2-68x)$ . Due to certain symmetries, the solution set of these equations is the union of the solution sets of  $14x+2\pi n=\pi/2-68x$  and  $14x+2\pi n=\pi/2+68x$ , which are  $x=\pi\frac{1+4n}{164}$  and  $x=\pi\frac{3+4n}{108}$ , respectively. Over the given interval, there are 82 solutions in the first set and 54 solutions in the second set. However, the solutions  $x=\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{3\pi}{2}$  are overcounted and can be verified to be the only overcounted solutions. Hence the answer is  $82+54-2=134\Longrightarrow\boxed{d}$ .

Prayers to all those who put (e) :(

stem_md:
Let  $n\ge3$  be an integer. A regular  $n$ -gon  $P$  is given. We randomly select three distinct vertices of  $P$ . The probability that these three vertices form an isosceles triangle is  $1/m$ , where  $m$  is an integer. How many such integers  $n\le 2024$  are there?
\[\rm a. ~674\qquad \mathrm b. ~675\qquad \mathrm c. ~682 \qquad\mathrm d. ~684\qquad\mathrm e. ~685\]
solution_md:
I think the only way to solve this problem is to separate it into cases. So far, the only cases that worked are  $n=3$ ,  $n=6k+4$  and  $n=6k+5$  , or maybe I miss some of them.
Denote  $A$  the number of isosceles triangles in the  $n$ -gon.

Case  $n=6k$ : $A=n(3k-1)-\frac{2}{3}(6k)=18k^2 - 10k=2k(9k-5)$  $P=\frac{2k(9k-5)}{\binom{n}{3}}=\frac{6\cdot2k(9k-5)}{6k(6k-1)(6k-2)}=\frac{9k-5}{(3k-1)(6k-1)}$ . 
Now, note that  $\gcd(9k-5, 3k-1) = \gcd(2, k-1)$  and  $\gcd(9k-5,6k-1)=\gcd(7, k+1)$ . Thus,  $9k-5$  equals to either  $1$ ,  $2$ ,  $7$  or  $14$ . None of the cases work, so  $n=6k$  has no solutions.

Case  $n=6k+1$ : $A=n(\lfloor \frac{n}{2}\rfloor)=n(3k)$  $P=\frac{3kn}{\binom{n}{3}}=\frac{6\cdot3kn}{n(n-1)(n-2)}=\frac{18k}{6k(6k-1)}=\frac{3}{6k-1}$ . 
Now, it's trivial that  $3 \nmid 6k-1$ , so  $\frac{3}{6k-1}$  cannot be represented as  $\frac{1}{m}$ . 

Case  $n=6k+2$ : $A=n(3k)$  $P=\frac{3kn}{\binom{n}{3}}=\frac{18kn}{n(n-1)(n-2)}=\frac{18k}{6k(6k+1)}=\frac{3}{6k+1}$ . 
Thus, case  $n=6k+2$  has no solutions.

Case  $n=6k+3$ : $A=n(3k+1)-\frac{2}{3}(6k+3)=(2k+1)(9k+1)$  $P=\frac{(2k+1)(9k+1)}{\binom{n}{3}}=\frac{6(2k+1)(9k+1)}{(6k+3)(6k+2)(6k+1)}=\frac{9k+1}{(3k+1)(6k+1)}$ . 
Now, note that  $\gcd(9k+1, 3k+1) = \gcd(2, k-1)$  and  $\gcd(9k+1,6k+1)=1$ . Thus,  $9k+1$  equals to either  $1$  or  $2$ , which is possible if and only if  $k=0$  and  $n=3$ .

Case  $n=6k+4$ : $A=n(3k+1)$  $P=\frac{n(3k+1)}{\binom{n}{3}}=\frac{6(3k+1)}{(n-1)(n-2)}=\frac{3(6k+2)}{(6k+3)(6k+2)}=\frac{1}{2k+1}$ ,  $m=2k+1$ .

Case  $n=6k+5$ : $A=n(3k+2)$  $P=\frac{n(3k+2)}{\binom{n}{3}}=\frac{6(3k+2)}{(n-1)(n-2)}=\frac{3(6k+4)}{(6k+4)(6k+3)}=\frac{1}{2k+1}$ ,  $m=2k+1$ .

----------------------------
In total, we have  $2\lfloor \frac{2024}{6} \rfloor + 1 = \boxed{675}$  solutions  $\Rightarrow \boxed{\textbf{b}}$

stem_md:
There are eight seats at a round table. Six adults  $A_1, \ldots, A_6$  and two children sit around the table. The two children are not allowed to six next to each other. All the seating configurations where the children are not seated next to each other are equally likely. What is the probability that the adults  $A_1$  and  $A_2$  end up sitting next to each other?\[
\mathrm a. ~4/15\qquad \mathrm b. ~2/7 \qquad \mathrm c. ~2/9 \qquad\mathrm d. ~1/3\qquad\mathrm e. ~1/5\qquad\]
solution_md:
Number the seats from  $1$  to  $8$  and WLOG that  $A_1$  takes seat  $1$ . The total number of seating configurations without regarding the restriction of children not sitting next to each other is  $7! = 5040$ . The total number of configurations where the two children sit next to each other is  $2 \cdot 6! = 1440$  (because we can view the two children as a single person and then permute everyone accounting for the order between children also). So, the number of "valid" configurations is  $3600$ . 

Now, we count the number of such configurations where  $A_1$  sits next to  $A_2$ . WLOG that  $A_2$  is on seat  $2$  and multiply by  $2$ . The number of ways for this is just  $6! - 2 \cdot 5! = 480$ . Then we multiply by  $2$  and get  $960$ . 

So the answer is \[ \frac{960}{3600} = \boxed{\text{a. }4/15} \]
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/USA Contests/USA - College-Hosted Events/UMD Math Competition/2024 UMD Math Competition Part I/3429056.json

stem_md:
How many real numbers  $a$  are there for which both solutions to the equation
\[x^2 + (a - 2024)x + a = 0\]
are integers?
\[\mathrm a. ~15\qquad \mathrm b. ~16 \qquad \mathrm c. ~18 \qquad\mathrm d. ~20\qquad\mathrm e. ~24\qquad\]
solution_md:
How many real numbers $a$ are there for which both solutions to the equation \[x^2 + (a - 2024)x + a = 0\] are integers? \[\mathrm a. ~15\qquad \mathrm b. ~16 \qquad \mathrm c. ~18 \qquad\mathrm d. ~20\qquad\mathrm e. ~24\qquad\]
So $m+n=2024-mn$ , which is $(m+1)(n+1)=2025=3^45^2$ with WLOG $m\ge n$ Since $2025$ has $15$ positive, divisors, one where $m=n$ and so $7$ where $m>n$ , there are $8$ such $mn$ where $m\ge n>0$ And same, there are $8$ such that $m\le n<0$ It is easy to show that these $16$ values for $a=mn$ all are distinct. Hence the answer $\boxed{16}$

stem_md:
Consider the sets  $A =  \{0,1,2\},$  and  $B = \{1,2,3,4,5\}.$  Find the number of functions  $f: A \to B$  such that  $x + f(x) + xf(x)$  is odd for all  $x.$  (A function  $f:A \to B$  is a rule that assigns to every number in  $A$  a number in  $B.$ )
\[\mathrm a. ~15\qquad \mathrm b. ~27 \qquad \mathrm c. ~30 \qquad\mathrm d. ~42\qquad\mathrm e. ~45\]
solution_md:
Claim:  $f$  works iff  $f$  of an even number is odd
Proof: To show that  $f$  of even is odd, plug  $x$  even and get the desired result. Now to show that everything works, note that  $x + f(x) + xf(x)$  is always odd for odd  $x$ , and it is odd for even  $x$  when  $f(x)$  is odd.  $\square$ Therefore, the answer is  $3 \cdot 3\cdot 5 = \boxed{\text{e.} \ 45}$ .
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/USA Contests/USA - College-Hosted Events/UMD Math Competition/2024 UMD Math Competition Part I/3432775.json

stem_md:
A square-shaped quilt is divided into  $16 = 4 \times 4$  equal squares. We say that the quilt is *UMD certified* if each of these  $16$  squares is colored red, yellow, or black, so that (i) all three colors are used at least once and (ii) the quilt looks the same when it is rotated  $90, 180,$  or  $270$  degrees about its center. How many distinct UMD certified quilts are there?
\[\rm a. ~33\qquad \mathrm b. ~36 \qquad \mathrm c. ~45\qquad\mathrm d. ~54\qquad\mathrm e. ~81\]
solution_md: It is easy to see that the quilt is determined by a coloring of a 2x2 grid. There are  $3^4=81$  colorings total.  $3\cdot 2^4=48$  of them use only 2 colorings, and  $3\cdot 1^4=3$  of them use only 1 color. By PIE, the answer is  $81-48+3=36\Longrightarrow\boxed{b}$ .

stem_md:
A square has  $2$  diagonals. A regular pentagon has  $5$  diagonals.  $n$  is the smallest positive integer such that a regular  $n$ -gon has greater than or equal to  $2024$  diagonals. What is the sum of the digits of  $n$ ?
\[\mathrm a. ~10\qquad \mathrm b. ~11 \qquad \mathrm c. ~12 \qquad\mathrm d. ~13\qquad\mathrm e. ~14\]
solution_md:
The number of diagonals is just  $\binom n2 - n$  (as the sides are not counted in the diagonals), so  $n$  works iff  $\binom n2 - n \ge 2024$ . Multiplying both sides by  $2$  gives an equivalence to \[n(n-1) - 2n \ge 4048 \iff n^2 - 3n \ge 4048 \iff 4n^2 - 12n \ge 16192 \iff (2n-3)^2 \ge 16201\]

Since  $127^2 < 16201 < 128^2$ , it is equivalent to  $(2n-3)^2 \ge 128^2$ , which for positive  $n$  implies  $n$  works iff  $2n - 3 \ge 128 \iff n \ge 66$  so the answer is  $\boxed{12}$ .
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/USA Contests/USA - College-Hosted Events/UMD Math Competition/2024 UMD Math Competition Part I/3437372.json

candidates:
One way of counting the diagonals in an  $n$ -gon is to consider the  $\binom{n}{2}$  possible line segments between any  $2$  points. Of these  $n$  will be the side-lengths of the polygon and not an interior diagonal, and so we consider  $\binom{n}{2}-n\geq 2024$ :  $$ \frac{n(n-3)}{2}\geq 2024 $$  Testing some cases above  $\approx \sqrt{2024}$  we find that  $n=66$  is the minimum such solution, giving  $c. \,12=6+6$  as the solution.

On the hunt for additional intuition: given  $n$  possible starting vertices there are  $n-3$  options for the next non-adjacent vertex to complete the diagonal. Dividing by two for the double-counting of points to lines gives  $n(n-3)/2$  as before.
Find minimum  $n$  from the equation   $$ \binom{n}{2}-n\geq2024 $$  You will get  $66$  and so sum of digits is  $12$ .

stem_md: Define two sequences  $x_n, y_n$  for  $n = 1, 2, \ldots$  by \[x_n = \left(\sum^n_{k=0} \binom{2n}{2k}49^k 48^{n-k} \right) -1, \quad \text{and} \quad y_n = \sum^{n-1}_{k=0} \binom{2n}{2k + 1} 49^k 48^{n-k}\] Prove there is a positive integer  $m$  for which for every integer  $n > m,$  the greatest common factor of  $x_n$  and  $y_n$  is more than  $10^{2024}.$
solution_md:
Let  $a = 7 + 4\sqrt{3}$  and  $b = 7 - 4\sqrt{3}$ . 

Claim:  $2(x_n + 1) = a^{2n} + b^{2n} $  and  $7y_n = 2\sqrt{3} (a^{2n} - b^{2n})$ . 
Proof: Omitted because it's banned.  $\square$ Now squaring the first equation and multiplying by  $12$  gives that  $48(x_n + 1)^2  = 12(a^{2n} + b^{2n})^2$  and squaring the second equation gives  $49 y_n^2 = 12 (a^{2n} - b^{2n})^2$ . 

Subtracting gives that  $48(x_n + 1)^2 - 49y_n^2 = 48$ . 

Thus,  $y_n^2 \mid 48x_n(x_n + 2)$ . 

Let  $d_n = \gcd(x_n, y_n)$  and  $y_n = d_n b_n $  and  $x_n = d_n a_n$ . 

We have  $d_n^2 b_n^2 \mid 48 d_n a_n(x_n + 2)$ , so \[ d_n b_n^2 \mid 48 a_n(x_n + 2)\] 

Since  $\gcd(a_n, b_n) = 1$ , \[ b_n^2 \mid 48(x_n + 2)\] Thus,  $x_n + 2 \ge \frac{b_n^2}{48} = \frac{y_n^2}{d_n^2 \cdot 48} $ . 

So  $48 = 48(x_n + 1)^2 - 49y_n^2 \ge 48(x_n + 1)^2 - d_n^2 \cdot  48 \cdot 49  \cdot (x_n + 2)$ . As  $n$  grows large,  $d_n$  must also grow large since  $x_n$  grows large, so for large enough  $n$ ,  $d_n > 10^{2024}$ .

stem_md: Prove for every positive integer  $n{:}$ \[ \frac {1 \cdot 3 \cdots (2n - 1)}{2 \cdot 4 \cdots (2n)} < \frac 1{\sqrt{3n}}\]
solution_md:
<details><summary>Hint 1</summary>If we directly try to use induction, it fails, as  $\frac{n+1}{n} > \frac{(2n+2)^2}{(2n+1)^2}$ .</details>
<details><summary>Hint 2</summary>Instead we can try to show that the LHS is at most  $\frac{1}{f(n)}$  such that  $f(n) > \sqrt{3n}$  and  $\frac{f(n+1)}{f(n)} < \frac{2n+2}{2n+1}$ .</details>
<details><summary>Solution</summary>We will actually show that for  $n\ge 2$ , the LHS is at most  $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3n+1}}$ . The base case  $n = 2$  is true, and then we induct. Notice that 
\[ \frac{3n+4}{3n+1} < \frac{(2n+2)^2}{(2n+1)^2} \iff 12n^3 + 28n^2 + 19n + 4 < 12n^3 + 28n^2 + 20n + 4 \]
which is enough to make the induction work.</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/USA Contests/USA - College-Hosted Events/UMD Math Competition/2024 UMD Math Competition Part II/3455928.json

candidates:
Take the reciprocal and square, it's equivalent to \[ \left( \frac{2 \cdot 4 \cdot \cdots  \cdot (2n)}{1 \cdot 3 \cdot \cdots \cdot (2n-1)} \right) ^2 > 3n\] 

Write the LHS as \[\frac{2}{1} \cdot \frac{2}{3} \cdot \frac{4}{3} \cdot \frac{4}{5} \cdot \frac{6}{5} \cdots \frac{2n-2}{2n-1} \cdot \frac{2n}{2n-1} \cdot 2n\] Now by the Wallis Product for  $\pi$ , this is more than  $\frac{\pi}{2} \cdot 2n = \pi n > 3n$ , as desired.

We show inductively the stronger
\[ \frac {1 \cdot 3 \cdots (2n - 1)}{2 \cdot 4 \cdots (2n)} \le \frac 1{\sqrt{3n+1}}\] so it suffices to show that

stem_md:
Consider a set  $S = \{a_1, \ldots, a_{2024}\}$  consisting of  $2024$  distinct positive integers that satisfies the following property:
[center] "For every positive integer  $m < 2024,$  the sum of no  $m$  distinct elements of  $S$  is a multiple of  $2024.$ " [/center]
Prove  $a_1, \ldots, a_{2024}$  all leave the same remainder when divided by  $2024.$  Justify your answer.
solution_md:
Consider an arbitrary permutation  $s_i$  of  $1,\dots,2024$  and consider the sequence given by  $b_1=a_{s_1},b_{n+1}=b_n+a_{s_{n+1}}$ .

By assumption,  $b_i,1\le i\le 2023$  are not  $0\pmod{2024}$ . If  $b_m\equiv b_n\pmod{2024},m>n$  then  $b_m-b_n=a_{s_{n+1}}+\dots+a_{s_m}\equiv 0\pmod{2024}$ .

Otherwise  $b_i,1\le i\le 2023$  are distinct  $\pmod{2024}$ , and thus congruent to some permutation of  $1,\dots,2023$ .

Now consider another permutation  $t_i$  so that  $s_1=t_2,s_2=t_1,s_n=t_n\forall 3\le n\le 2024$ . Then if we have  $c_1=a_{t_1},c_{n+1}=c_n+a_{t_{n+1}}$  then we can assume  $c_i,1\le i\le 2023$  is congruent to a permutation of  $1,\dots,2023$ .

However  $b_n=c_n\forall 2\le n\le 2024$ , so  $b_1\equiv c_1\pmod{2024}\implies a_{s_1}\equiv a_{t_1}\pmod{2024}$ . Since  $s_1,t_1=s_2$  are arbitrary, we get all  $a_i$  equal  $\pmod{2024}$ .

stem_md: A right triangle  $A_1 A_2 A_3$  with side lengths  $6,\,8,$  and  $10$  on a plane  $\mathcal P$  is given. Three spheres  $S_1,S_2$  and  $S_3$  with centers  $O_1, O_2,$  and  $O_3,$  respectively, are located on the same side of the plane  $\mathcal P$  in such a way that  $S_i$  is tangent to  $\mathcal P$  at  $A_i$  for  $i = 1, 2, 3.$  Assume  $S_1, S_2, S_3$  are pairwise externally tangent. Find the area of triangle  $O_1O_2O_3.$
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Let the radius of  $O_i$  be  $r_i$ . Then taking cross sections  $O_1O_2A_1A_2$  and the obvious cyclic other cross sections, they are right trapezoids, and we find that  $r_1r_2 = 9$ ,  $r_2r_3 = 16$  and  $r_3r_1 = 25$  (without loss of generality). This gives  $r_1 = \frac{15}{4}$ ,  $r_2 = \frac{12}{5}$  and  $r_3 = \frac{20}{3}$ .

Notice that  $[O_1O_2O_3]$  has side lengths  $r_1 + r_2$ ,  $r_2 + r_3$  and  $r_3 + r_1$ . We can use Heron's and find that 
\[ O_1O_2O_3 = \sqrt{ (r_1 + r_2 + r_3) \cdot r_1 \cdot r_2 \cdot r_3} \] 
which comes out to  $\sqrt{769}$ .</details>

stem_md:
Find the largest positive integer  $n$  satisfying the following:
[center]

"There are precisely  $53$  integers in the list of integers  $1, 2, \ldots, n$  that are either perfect squares, perfect cubes or both."[/center]
solution_md:
Let $f(n)$ be the number of elements of $\{1,2,\ldots, n\}$ that are squares, cubes, or both. Note that $f$ is nondecreasing and, $f(n+1) = f(n) + 1$ iff $n+1$ is a square or a cube. Claim: $f(2024) = 53$ . Proof: Follows because $f(2024) = 44 + 12 - 3 = 53$ . $\square$ Now note that $2025$ is a square, so $f(2025) = 54$ . This means for any $x > 2024$ , $f(x) \ge f(2025) = 54$ , so $f(x) > 53$ , meaning $\boxed{2024}$ is maximal.
The $f$ here is $f(n)=\left \lfloor \sqrt{n}\right \rfloor +\left \lfloor \sqrt[3]{n}\right \rfloor -\left \lfloor \sqrt[6]{n}\right \rfloor$ . Now we do *olympiad* problem solving and guess that the answer should be something around $2025$ , motivated by the fact that this is a perfect square. We compute $f(2025)=45+12-3=54$ , and since $2025$ is a perfect square, we get $f(2024)=53$ . Now, $f$ is clearly nondecreasing (because the number of elements that satisfy the conditions from $\{1,\ldots ,n+1\}$ is at least the number of elements that satisfy the condition from $\{1,\ldots ,n\}$ ). Hence the largest such $n$ is $2024$ .

candidates: <details><summary>1a</summary>There has to be a power of 5 somewhere since it is odd. We experiment with 125 and see that the remaining sum is 282. 250 + 32 looks like a good guess and indeed the product of these 3 is 1000000.</details>

<details><summary>Solution for p1(b)</summary>Note that the product must have at least  $7$  powers of  $5.$ Clearly, not all powers of  $5$  can be in the same number, because then it would be way too big.

If all the powers of  $5$  are in only two of the numbers, then, by the Pigeonhole Principle, one of them has at least  $4$  powers of  $5.$  However, that number must be at least  $625,$  which is too big as well.

Hence, each of the numbers must have at least  $1$  power of  $5.$  However, this means that their sum must be divisible by  $5,$  contradiction.

Therefore, we can conclude that there does **not** exist positive integers  $a,b,c$  whose sum is  $407$  and whose product ends in seven  $0$ 's.  $\square$</details>
<details><summary>Solution for p4(a)</summary>Assume, for the sake of contradiction, that the number of employees with an odd number of acquaintances is odd.

When we add up the number of acquaintances for each employee, the total quantity will double-count each acquaintance, so it must be even.

However, if the number of employees with an odd number of acquaintances is odd, then if we add up the number of acquaintances for each employee, the total quantity will be odd, contradiction. 

Hence, we can conclude that the number of employees at Gigafirm with an odd number of acquaintances must be even.  $\square$</details>
<details><summary>Note for p4(a)</summary>In Graph Theory, this translates to the [Handshaking Lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handshaking_lemma).</details>
<details><summary>Solution for p4(b)</summary>It suffices to prove that every person must get an even number of letters.

If someone has an odd number of acquaintances, we can use casework* to show that they will get an odd number of letters from other people and a letter from themself, for a total of an even number of letters.

If someone has an even number of acquaintances, we can use casework* to show that they will get an even number of letters from other people and they will not get a letter from themself, for a total of an even number of letters, so we are done.  $\square$ *The cases are on the parity of the number of acquaintances of that person that have an odd number of acquaintances and the parity of the number of acquaintances of that person that have an even number of acquaintances. (There are  $4$  cases in total.)</details>

The triangle shown is magic because  $4 = 1 + 3$ ,  $5 = 3 + 2$ , and  $9 = 4 + 5$ .  $$ 9 $$    $$ 4\,\,\,\,5 $$    $$ 1\,\,\,\,3\,\,\,\,2 $$  (a) Find a magic triangle such that the numbers at the three corners are  $10$ ,  $20$ , and  $2010$ , with  $2010$  at the top.
(b) Find a magic triangle such that the numbers at the three corners are  $20$ ,  $201$ , and  $2010$ , with  $2010$  at the top, or prove that no such triangle exists.**p2.** (a) The equalities  $\frac12+\frac13+\frac16= 1$  and  $\frac12+\frac13+\frac17+\frac{1}{42}= 1$  express  $1$  as a sum of the reciprocals
of three (respectively four) distinct positive integers. Find five positive integers  $a < b < c <d < e$  such that  $$ \frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}+\frac{1}{d}+\frac{1}{e}= 1. $$  (b) Prove that for any integer  $m \ge 3$ , there exist  $m$  positive integers  $d_1 < d_2 <... < d_m$  such that   $$ \frac{1}{d_1}+\frac{1}{d_2}+ ... +\frac{1}{d_m}= 1. $$  **p3.** Suppose that  $P(x) = a_nx^n +... + a_1x + a_0$  is a polynomial of degree n with real coefficients. Say that the real number  $b$  is a balance point of  $P$  if for every pair of real numbers  $a$  and  $c$  such that  $b$  is the average of  $a$  and  $c$ , we have that  $P(b)$  is the average of  $P(a)$  and  $P(c)$ . Assume that  $P$  has two distinct balance points. Prove that  $n$  is at most  $1$ , i.e., that  $P$  is a linear function.**p4.** A roller coaster at an amusement park has a train consisting of  $30$  cars, each seating two people next to each other.  $60$  math students want to take as many rides as they can, but are told that there are two rules that cannot be broken. First, all  $60$  students must ride each time, and second, no two students are ever allowed to sit next to each other more than once. What is the maximal number of roller coaster rides that these students can take? Justify your answer.**p5.** Let  $ABCD$  be a convex quadrilateral such that the lengths of all four sides and the two diagonals of  $ABCD$  are rational numbers. If the two diagonals  $AC$  and  $BD$  intersect at a point  $M$ , prove that the length of  $AM$  is also a rational number.

**p1.** You are given three buckets with a capacity to hold  $8$ ,  $5$ , and  $3$  quarts of water, respectively. Initially, the first bucket is filled with  $8$  quarts of water, while the remaining two buckets are empty. There are no markings on the buckets, so you are only allowed to empty a bucket into another one or to fill a bucket to its capacity using the water from one of the other buckets.
(a) Describe a procedure by which we can obtain exactly  $6$  quarts of water in the first bucket.
(b) Describe a procedure by which we can obtain exactly  $4$  quarts of water in the first bucket.**p2.** A point in the plane is called a lattice point if its coordinates are both integers. A triangle whose vertices are all lattice points is called a lattice triangle. In each case below, give explicitly the coordinates of the vertices of a lattice triangle  $T$  that satisfies the stated properties.
(a) The area of  $T$  is  $1/2$  and two sides of  $T$  have length greater than  $2011$ .
(b) The area of  $T$  is  $1/2$  and the three sides of  $T$  each have length greater than  $2011$ .**p3.** Alice and Bob play several rounds of a game. In the  $n$ -th round, where  $n = 1, 2, 3, ...$ , the loser pays the winner  $2^{n-1}$  dollars (there are no ties). After  $40$  rounds, Alice has a profit of  $\$ 2011 $ (and Bob has lost $ \ $2011$ ). How many rounds of the game did Alice win, and which rounds were they? Justify your answer.**p4.** Each student in a school is assigned a  $15$ -digit ID number consisting of a string of  $3$ ’s and  $7$ ’s. Whenever  $x$  and  $y$  are two distinct ID numbers, then  $x$  and  $y$  differ in at least three entries. Show that the number of students in the school is less than or equal to  $2048$ .**p5.** A triangle  $ABC$  has the following property: there is a point  $P$  in the plane of  $ABC$  such that the triangles  $PAB$ ,  $PBC$  and  $PCA$  all have the same perimeter and the same area. Prove that:
(a) If  $P$  is not inside the triangle  $ABC$ , then  $ABC$  is a right-angled triangle.
(b) If  $P$  is inside the triangle  $ABC$ , then  $ABC$  is an equilateral triangle.

**p1.** (a) Suppose  $101$  Dalmatians chase  $2012$  squirrels. Each squirrel gets chased by at most one Dalmatian, and each Dalmatian chases at least one squirrel. Show that two Dalmatians chase the same number of squirrels.
(b) What is the largest number of Dalmatians that can chase  $2012$  squirrels in a way that each Dalmatian chases at least one squirrel and no two Dalmatians chase the same number of squirrels?**p2.** Lucy and Linus play the following game. They start by putting the integers  $1, 2, 3, ..., 2012$  in a hat. In each round of the game, Lucy and Linus each draw a number from the hat. If the two numbers are  $a$  and  $b$ , they throw away these numbers and put the number  $|a - b|$  back into the hat. After  $2011$  rounds, there is only one number in the hat. If it is even, Lucy wins. If it is odd, Linus wins.
(a) Prove that there is a sequence of drawings that makes Lucy win.
(b) Prove that Lucy always wins.**p3.** Suppose  $x$  is a positive real number and  $x^{1990}$ ,  $x^{2001}$ , and  $x^{2012}$  differ by integers. Prove that  $x$  is an integer.**p4.** Suppose that each point in three-dimensional space is colored with one of five colors and suppose that each color is used at least once. Prove that there is some plane that contains at least four of the colors.**p5.** Two circles,  $C_1$  and  $C_2$ , are tangent at point  $A$ , with  $C_1$  lying inside  $C_2$  (and  $C_1 \ne C_2$ ). The line through their centers intersects  $C_1$  at  $B_1$  and  $C_2$  at  $B_2$ . A line  $L$  is drawn through  $A$  and it intersects  $C_1$  at  $P_1$  (with  $P_1 \ne A$ ) and intersects  $C_2$  at  $P_2$  (with  $P_2 \ne A$ ). The perpendicular from  $P_2$  to the line  $B_1B_2$  intersects the line  $B_1B_2$  at  $F$ . Prove that if the line  $P_1F$  is tangent to  $C_1$  then  $F$  is the midpoint of the line segment  $B_1B_2$ .
![Image](https://cdn.artofproblemsolving.com/attachments/9/e/4db59be9fa764d3e910a828ed3296907ca5657.png)


PS. You should use hide for answers. Collected [here](https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c5h2760506p24143309).
solution_md:
P3

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>Let  $D_1=x^{2012}-x^{2001}= x^{2001}(x^{11}-1) \in Z$  $D_2=x^{2001}-x^{1990}= x^{1990}(x^{11}-1) \in Z$  $\Longrightarrow D_1-D_2= x^{2012}-x^{2001}-(x^{2001}-x^{1990})= (x^{2001}-x^{1990})(x^{11}-1)\in Z$  $\Rightarrow (x^{11}-1)\in Z \Rightarrow x^{11} \in Z$ (see second equation)  $\Longrightarrow x^{1990}\in Z$ .

If  $ x^{11} \in Q , x^{1990} \in Q $  $\Longrightarrow x= \frac{[x^{11}]^{181}}{x^{1990}}=\frac{x^{1991}}{x^{1990}} \in Q$ .

Assuming that  $x=\frac{p}{q}, (p,q)=1, p<q\Longrightarrow x^{2001}(x^{11}-1) <1$  (not in Z, contradicting first equation)

If  $p>q\Longrightarrow x^{11}=\frac{p^{11}}{q^{11}}$  not in  $Z$ , contradicting the finding that  $x^{11} \in Z$ In conclusion  $x\in Z$</details>

**p1.** A *multimagic* square is a  $3 \times 3$  array of distinct positive integers with the property that the product of the  $3$  numbers in each row, each column, and each of the two diagonals of the array is always the same.
(a) Prove that the numbers  $1, 2, 3, . . . , 9$  cannot be used to form a multimagic square.
(b) Give an example of a multimagic square.**p2.** A sequence  $a_1, a_2, a_3, ... , a_n$  of real numbers is called an arithmetic progression if   $$ a_1 - a_2 = a_2 - a_3 = ... = a_{n-1} - a_n. $$  Prove that there exist distinct positive integers  $n_1, n_2, n_3, ... , n_{2014}$  such that   $$ \frac{1}{n_1},\frac{1}{n_2}, ... ,\frac{1}{n_{2014}} $$   is an arithmetic progression.**p3.** Let  $\lfloor x \rfloor$   be the largest integer that is less than or equal to  $x$ . For example,   $\lfloor 3.9 \rfloor  = 3$  and   $\lfloor 4\rfloor  = 4$ . Determine (with proof) all real solutions of the equation   $$ x^2 - 25 \lfloor x\rfloor + 100 = 0. $$  **p4.** An army has  $10$  cannons and  $8$  carts. Each cart can carry at most one cannon. It takes one day for a cart to cross the desert. What is the least number of days that it takes to get the cannons across the desert? (Cannons can be left part way and picked up later during the procedure.) Prove that the amount of time that your solution requires to move the cannons across the desert is the smallest possible.**p5.** Let  $C$  be a convex polygon with  $4031$  sides. Let  $p$  be the length of its perimeter and let  $d$  be the sum of the lengths of its diagonals. Show that   $$ \frac{d}{p}> 2014. $$  PS. You should use hide for answers. Collected [here](https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c5h2760506p24143309).

= \frac{k - 2000}{15}+\frac{k - 2003}{12}+\frac{k - 2006}{9}+\frac{k - 2009}{6}+\frac{k - 2012}{3}. $$  **p3.** Some (not necessarily distinct) natural numbers from  $1$  to  $2015$  are written on  $2015$  lottery tickets, with exactly one number written on each ticket. Prove that the same number is written on all of the tickets.**p4.** A set of points  $A$  is called distance-distinct if every pair of points in  $A$  has a different distance.
(a) Show that for all infinite sets of points  $B$  on the real line, there exists an infinite distance-distinct set A contained in  $B$ .
(b) Show that for all infinite sets of points  $B$  on the real plane, there exists an infinite distance-distinct set A contained in  $B$ .**p5.** Let  $ABCD$  be a (not necessarily regular) tetrahedron and consider six points  $E, F, G, H, I, J$  on its edges  $AB$ ,  $BC$ ,  $AC$ ,  $AD$ ,  $BD$ ,  $CD$ , respectively, such that   $$ |AE| \cdot |EB| = |BF| \cdot |FC| = |AG| \cdot |GC| = |AH| \cdot |HD| = |BI| \cdot |ID| = |CJ| \cdot |JD|. $$   Prove that the points  $E, F, G, H, I$ , and  $J$  lie on the surface of a sphere.

Let $ D $ and $ E $ be the midpoints of the line segments $ AB $ and $ AC $. Prove that the line DE does not intersect the circle.**p3.** Let $ n \ge 2 $ be an integer. A subset $ S $ of {0, 1, . . . , n − 2} is said to be closed whenever it satisfies all of the following properties:
• $ 0 \in S $
• If $ x \in S $ then $ n - 2 - x \in S $
• If $ x \in S $, $ y \ge 0 $, and $ y + 1 $ divides $ x + 1 $ then $ y \in S $.
Prove that $ \{0, 1, . . . , n - 2\} $ is the only closed subset if and only if $ n $ is prime.
(Note: “$ \in $” means “belongs to”.)**p4.** Consider the $ 3 \times 3 $ grid shown below
$ \begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
 A  &  B & C  \hline
 D &  E &    F   \hline
G &  H  &  I   \hline
\end{tabular} $

<details><summary>Solution for p1</summary>If  $\lfloor x\rfloor \leq 34,$  then   $$ x\lfloor x \rfloor < 35\cdot34=1190<1234, $$   contradiction.

If  $\lfloor x \rfloor \geq 36,$  then   $$ x\lfloor x \rfloor \geq 36\cdot36=1296>1234, $$   contradiction.

stem_md: Prove that among any  $12$  consecutive positive integers there is at least one which is smaller than the sum of its proper divisors. (The proper divisors of a positive integer n are all positive integers other than  $1$  and  $n$  which divide  $n$ . For example, the proper divisors of  $14$  are  $2$  and  $7$ .)
solution_md: <details><summary>solution</summary>Let  $n\in \mathbb{Z}^+.$  Then the numbers are in the form  $12n-11,12n-10, \cdots, 12n.$  Since  $n, 2n, 3n, 4n,$  and  $6n$  are divisors of  $12n,$  and their sum is  $16n,$  since  $16n > 12n,$  we are done.  $\blacksquare$</details>

stem_md: Finitely many cards are placed in two stacks, with more cards in the left stack than the right. Each card has one or more distinct names written on it, although different cards may share some names. For each name, we define a “shuffle” by moving every card that has this name written on it to the opposite stack. Prove that it is always possible to end up with more cards in the right stack by picking several distinct names, and doing in turn the shuffle corresponding to each name.

*Where the exponentiation $x^{\tau_i(c)}$ is $1$ if $\tau_i(c)=_{\mathbb F_2} 0$ and $x$ if $\tau_i(c)=_{\mathbb F_2} 1$*
A passing thought—this is not quite "ḥalāl" as is suggested by the failure of the naïve expectation that $1=x^0=x^{1+1}=x^1\cdot x^1=x^2$ . The proper thing to do (essentially to force reality to conform to our delusion) is to work over $\overline{\mathbb Q}[x]/(x^2-1)$ so that the identity $x^{a_1b_1+a_2b_2}=\left(x^{a_1}\right)^{b_1}\left(x^{a_2}\right)^{b_2}$ respects the structure of $\mathbb F_2$ . Making use of the fact that $T_c>0$ , the pertinent generating function is then again $$ \text{P}:=\prod_{i\in\{1,\dots,d\}} \tfrac{1}{2}+\tfrac{1}{2}x^{\tau_i(c)}=\prod_{\tau_i(c)=_{\mathbb F_2}1}\tfrac{1}{2}+\tfrac{1}{2}x^{\tau_i(c)}=\left(\tfrac{1}{2}+\tfrac{1}{2}x^{\tau_i(c)}\right)^{T_c} $$ of which we would like to extract the "constant" term modulo $x^2-1$ (the word "constant" being treated with the appropriate amount of caution). A clue as to how to proceed comes from the Chinese Remainder Theorem, with $\overline{\mathbb Q}[x]/(x^2-1)\cong \overline{\mathbb Q}[x]/(x-1)\times \overline{\mathbb Q}[x]/(x+1)$ . In particular, the residues of $\text{P}$ evaluated at the canonical projection unto each factor (given by evaluation at $1$ and $-1$ respectively) is sufficient data to recover that of $\text{P}$ mod $x^2-1$ . Computing, $$ \text{P}=\text{P}(1)=1\pmod{\overline{\mathbb Q}[x]/(x-1)} $$ $$ \text{P}=\text{P}(-1)=0\pmod{\overline{\mathbb Q}[x]/(x+1)} $$ Now for any residue class $a_0+a_1x\in \overline{\mathbb Q}[x]/(x^2-1)$ , the projections onto $\overline{\mathbb Q}[x]/(x-1)$ and $\overline{\mathbb Q}[x]/(x+1)$ are $a_0+a_1$ and $a_0-a_1$ respectively, so it follows with a (very) small amount of linear algebra that $$ \text{P}=_{\overline{\mathbb Q}[x]/(x^2-1)}\tfrac{\text{P}(1)+\text{P}(-1)}{2}+\tfrac{\text{P}(1)-\text{P}(-1)}{2}x=\tfrac{1}{2}+\tfrac{1}{2}x $$ And at long last we find that the coefficient of $x^0$ is just $\boxed{\tfrac{1}{2}}$ , precisely as claimed $\Box$ ------------------------------ It is straightforward to replace $2$ with arbitrary positive integer $n$ and vector space $\mathbb F_2$ with module $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ . The polynomial $x^n-1$ remains squarefree in the general, and the operant isomorphism of rings therefore becomes $$ \overline{\mathbb Q}[x]/(x^n-1)\cong \prod_{k=0}^{n-1} \overline{\mathbb Q}[x]/(x-e^{\frac{2\pi i k}{n}}) $$ with canonical projections evaluated as before—namely by plugging in the $n^{\text{th}}$ roots of unity and then performing the appropriate linear algebra to extract the coefficient of interest. Of course, this is nothing other than the usual root of unity filter "trick," which turns out to be not at all a "trick" but rather quite motivated for deep reasons.

If the cards are  $\{x,y,z\}$  then  $S$  is the space of functions  $\{x,y,z\}\to \mathbb F_2$  and if the piles are  $\text{L}=\{x,y\}$  and  $\text{R}=\{z\}$  then the current state is the function that maps   $$ x\mapsto 0,\ y\mapsto 0,\ z\mapsto 1 $$   which happens to be the basis element  $\chi_z$ . With regards to your second question, the most truthful answer is perhaps that I’m simply not very good at finding monovariants (or any other, more “standard,” combinatorial arguments really). But beyond that, I personally find there to be two principal motivating ideas at play: the first is that the “shuffle” operations commute with one another and reverse themselves. This happens to be exactly the same thing as saying that the collection of possible transformations has a structure of a vector space over  $\mathbb F_2$  with addition composition , and once this is clear it is easy to see the overlying space  $S$  of states upon which the transformations are acting. The second notion is that of balance—we are told that something starts out on one (the left) end of some spectrum and  want to show that it is possible to move it to the opposite (right) end of “the spectrum”. The classical nonconstructive approach to doing so (and it is clear after some playing around that a constructive approach will be tedious at best, impossibly hard to realize at worst) is to leverage the probabilistic method by showing that when averaged over *all* possibilities, the “thing” occupies the exact middle of the spectrum—that the spectrum is balanced, and thus that any deviation to one side (as is the initial state of the problem above) must be met with some deviation to the opposing side—exactly the feature whose existence we are tasked with demonstrating.

From time to time you rub so the liquid penetrates better, and otherwise you let time pass. The shell becomes more flexible through weeks and months—when the time is ripe, hand pressure is enough, the shell opens like a perfectly ripened avocado.
In math contests there is a rather definite weightiness given to the former style—what [Gowers](https://www.dpmms.cam.ac.uk/~wtg10/2cultures.pdf) would likely deem the "problem solver's approach"—and to be sure I am in no way attacking this preference. In many ways it is an inevitable corollary of the ideal that olympiads should be as accessible and as free of requisite background in higher mathematics as is achievable (whether or not this ideal is reflected in the actual state of olympiad mathematics is up for debate, but certainly it is by no means required that one have knowledge of [coherent sheaves on noetherian schemes](https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h1480686p8648257) in order to solve IMO problems). And indeed, mathematics (and truly almost every aspect of human endeavor) needs those with adept problem solving skills. But there is equally much good to be said for the complementary approach, that of the nut left to steep in water, of the "rising sea" as it insensibly advances on some hard marl. In particular, as a student of higher math I find that this perspective helps me contextualize the problems I encounter, and more (most) importantly, the subtle *theories*—not *theorems*—that they expose at play. (Note: I'm like 100% sure the theory/theorem pun is due to **pythag011** but I can't find the original post so I'll just link [this one](https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c170h491865p2759417) instead.) One of the things I enjoy the most about frequenting this forum is the rich profusion of novel perspective one is afforded from reading others' posted solutions. I am thus delighted by the proposition that I may for another have done the same.

We view the relation between cards and names as a bipartite graph, the set of vertices are  $C$  (cards) and  $N$  (names), and each  $c\in C$  is connected with at least one  $n\in N$ . The vertices in  $C$  are distributed into two containers  $C_1,C_2$ . Initially  $C_1$  contains  $k$  elements and  $C_2$  -  $\ell$  elements,  $k>\ell$ . 
	At every step we pick  $n\in N$  and all  $c\in C_1$  , which are connected with  $n$  are transferred into  $C_2$  and vice versa. 
	Let  $N'\subset N$  be the set of chosen names. The order they are picked doesn't matter for the final result. A vertex  $c\in C$  is transferred into other container iff  $\left|\{n\in N' : c\text{ is connected with }n \}\right|$  is odd.   
	
	Suppose we pick randomly the set of vertices  $N'\subset N$  (each with chance  $1/2$ ). For a fixed vertex  $c\in C$  the chance of being transferred equals the chance odd number of vertices in  $N(c)$  being chosen. ( $N(c)$  denotes the set of neighbours of  $c$ ). Since  $N(c)\neq \emptyset$ , that chance is  $1/2$ .
	By linearity of expectation, the expected number of vertices, initially in  $C_1$  , that are transferred into  $C_2$  is exactly  $k/2$ . In the same way, the expected number of vertices transferred from  $C_2$  to  $C_1$  is  $\ell/2$ . 
	Thus, the expected number of vertices that finally appear in each container is  $(k+\ell)/2$ , which means equal. 
	
	Since when  $N'=\emptyset$  ,  $C_1$  contains more elements than  $C_2$  , there must exist a set  $N'\subset N$  for which  $C_2$  contains more elements than  $C_1$ . 
	
	**Comment**. As I see, this is virtually the same approach as in #2 (rafayaashary1).

stem_md:
Alice plays the following game of solitaire on a  $20 \times 20$  chessboard. 
She begins by placing  $100$  pennies,  $100$  nickels,  $100$  dimes, and  $100$  quarters on the board so that each of the  $400$  squares contains exactly one coin. She then chooses  $59$  of these coins and removes them from the board. 
After that, she removes coins, one at a time, subject to the following rules:
- A penny may be removed only if there are four squares of the board adjacent to its square (up, down, left, and right) that are vacant (do not contain coins). Squares “off the board” do not count towards this four: for example, a non-corner square bordering the edge of the board has three adjacent squares, so a penny in such a square cannot be removed under this rule, even if all three adjacent squares are vacant.
- A nickel may be removed only if there are at least three vacant squares adjacent to its square. (And again, “off the board” squares do not count.)
- A dime may be removed only if there are at least two vacant squares adjacent to its square (“off the board” squares do not count).
- A quarter may be removed only if there is at least one vacant square adjacent to its square (“off the board” squares do not count).
Alice wins if she eventually succeeds in removing all the coins. Prove that it is impossiblefor her to win.

stem_md: Prove that there exists a set  $S$  of  $3^{1000}$  points in the plane such that for each point  $P$  in  $S$ , there are at least  $2000$  points in  $S$  whose distance to  $P$  is exactly  $1$  inch.
solution_md:
Iteratively build sets  $S_n$ , which have  $3^n$  points each of whom have  $2n$  points which are 1 unit away.  $S_1$  can be constructed by taking a unit equilateral triangle.

For the iterative step, construct  $S_{n+1} = \{ S_n, S_n + z, S_n + z\cdot \text{cis}(60)\}$  where  $z$  is a complex number with magnitude 1 such that  $S_n, S_n+z, S_n + z\cdot \text{cis}(60)$  do not intersect. This clearly gives 2 two new neighbors to each point, so each point in  $S_{n+1}$  now has  $2(n+1)$  neighbors.  $\blacksquare$ .

stem_md: Let  $x_1, x_2, ..., x_n$  be positive numbers, with  $n \ge 2$ . Prove that  $$ \left(x_1+\frac{1}{x_1}\right)\left(x_2+\frac{1}{x_2}\right)...\left(x_n+\frac{1}{x_n}\right)\ge \left(x_1+\frac{1}{x_2}\right)\left(x_2+\frac{1}{x_3}\right)...\left(x_{n-1}+\frac{1}{x_n}\right)\left(x_n+\frac{1}{x_1}\right) $$
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>We proceed with induction on  $n$ . The base case  $n=2$  is 
\[\left(x_1+\frac{1}{x_1}\right)\left(x_2+\frac{1}{x_2}\right) \geq \left(x_1+\frac{1}{x_2}\right)\left(x_2+\frac{1}{x_1}\right),\]
or
\begin{align*}
x_1 x_2+\frac{x_1}{x_2}+\frac{x_2}{x_1}+\frac{1}{x_1 x_2}  &\geq x_1 x_2+\frac{1}{x_1 x_2}+2 
\frac{x_1}{x_2}+\frac{x_2}{x_1} &\geq 2,
\end{align*}
which is true by the AM-GM Inequality.

For the inductive hypothesis, we assume the inequality holds for  $n=k$  and prove the inequality holds for  $n=k+1$ . We wish to prove that   $$ \left(x_1+\frac{1}{x_1}\right)\left(x_2+\frac{1}{x_2}\right)...\left(x_{n+1}+\frac{1}{x_{n+1}}\right)\ge \left(x_1+\frac{1}{x_2}\right)\left(x_2+\frac{1}{x_3}\right)...\left(x_{n}+\frac{1}{x_{n+1}}\right)\left(x_{n+1}+\frac{1}{x_1}\right). $$  Without loss of generality, let  $x_1>x_2>\cdots x_{n+1}$ . By our inductive hypothesis,  $$ \left(x_1+\frac{1}{x_1}\right)\left(x_2+\frac{1}{x_2}\right)...\left(x_n+\frac{1}{x_n}\right)\ge \left(x_1+\frac{1}{x_2}\right)\left(x_2+\frac{1}{x_3}\right)...\left(x_{n-1}+\frac{1}{x_n}\right)\left(x_n+\frac{1}{x_1}\right). $$  Multiplying both sides by  $\left(x_{n+1}+\frac{1}{x_{n+1}}\right)$ , we have   $$ \left(x_1+\frac{1}{x_1}\right)\left(x_2+\frac{1}{x_2}\right)...\left(x_{n+1}+\frac{1}{x_{n+1}}\right)\ge \left(x_1+\frac{1}{x_2}\right)\left(x_2+\frac{1}{x_3}\right)...\left(x_{n-1}+\frac{1}{x_{n+1}}\right)\left(x_{n}+\frac{1}{x_1}\right)\left(x_{n+1}+\frac{1}{x_{n+1}}\right). $$  We claim the right hand side is greater than or equal to  $$ \left(x_1+\frac{1}{x_2}\right)\left(x_2+\frac{1}{x_3}\right)...\left(x_{n}+\frac{1}{x_{n+1}}\right)\left(x_{n+1}+\frac{1}{x_1}\right) $$  which will finish the induction.

Proving this is equivalent to proving the following:  $$ \left(x_{n}+\frac{1}{x_1}\right)\left(x_{n+1}+\frac{1}{x_{n+1}}\right) \geq \left(x_{n}+\frac{1}{x_{n+1}}\right)\left(x_{n+1}+\frac{1}{x_1}\right), $$  or   $$ \frac{x_n}{x_{n+1}} + \frac{x_{n+1}}{x_1} \geq \frac{x_n}{x_1}+1. $$  We shall proceed with the inequality  $x_1\geq x_{n+1}$  which we defined. Taking the reciprocal and multiplying both sides by  $\left(x_n-x_{n+1}\right)$ , we have  $$ \frac{x_n-x_{n+1}}{x_{n+1}} \geq \frac{x_n-x_{n+1}}{x_1}. $$  Splitting the terms and rearranging, we have  $$ \frac{x_n}{x_{n+1}} + \frac{x_{n+1}}{x_1} \geq \frac{x_n}{x_1}+1. $$  This finishes our induction  $\square$</details>

stem_md:
Let  $f (n)$  be a function satisfying the following three conditions for all positive integers  $n$ :
(a)  $f (n)$  is a positive integer,
(b)  $f (n + 1) > f (n)$ ,
(c)  $f ( f (n)) = 3n$ .
Find  $f (2001)$ .
solution_md:
Nice problem! :)

We have  $f(f(n))=3n\implies f(f(f(n)))=f(3n)\implies 3f(n)=f(3n)$ . This will be used heavily throughout the solution. 
Condition (c) tells us that the function is surjective over the positive integral multiple of  $3$ .
Now suppose that  $f(1)=a$ . Then we have  $f(3)=3a$ . Now observe that if  $a\ge 4$ , there must exist at-least 2 multiples of 3 between  $a$  and  $3a$ . This leads to a contradiction because all those multiple of 3 values must be achievable by  $f(2)$ .**Case 1:**  $f(1)=3$ This implies  $f(3)=9$ .  So  $f(2)=6$ . But we know that  $f(f(2))=6\implies f(6)=6\implies f(f(6))=f(6)=6\ne 18$ , a contradiction.**Case 2:**  $f(1)=1$ It's not hard to eliminate this case using condition (c) alone.**Case 3:**  $f(1)=2$ By brute force we can find that  $f(8)=15$  and  $f(25)=48$ . Thus  $f(72)=135$  and  $f(75)=144$ . So  $f(74)=141\implies f(666)=9f(74)=9\times 141=1269$ Again,  $f(222)=3f(74)=3\times 141= 423$  and  $f(225)=3f(75)=3\times 144=432$ . So  $f(223)=426\implies f(669)=3\times 426=1278$ .

Thus we get  $f(667)=1272\implies f(2001)=3816$ .

stem_md: A game is played with two players and an initial stack of  $n$  pennies  $(n \geq 3)$ . The players take turns choosing one of the stacks of pennies on the table and splitting it into two stacks. The winner is the player who makes a move that causes all stacks to be of height  $1$  or  $2.$  For which starting values of n does the player who goes first win, assuming best play by both players?
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>We claim that the first player wins if and only if  $n=3$  or  $n$  is even.
First, if  $n=3$ , the first player wins by splitting the stack into stacks of size  $1$  and  $2$ .
Now, let a *fancy stack* be a stack that can be split (i.e. A stack with at least  $2$  pennies), let a *fancy penny* be a penny in any fancy stack, and let a *fancy position* be a position such that all of the stacks have an odd number of pennies, and such that if there is exactly one fancy stack, that stack has more than  $3$  pennies. Note that any move decreases the number of fancy pennies by the number of new stacks of size  $1$  (possibly none). Then, we will show the following lemma:**Lemma:** In any fancy position, the next player (i.e. The player who has his/her turn right now) loses.**Proof:** Assume for contradiction that there is a fancy position such that the next player can win. Let us consider such a position with a minimal number of fancy pennies. Then, we use casework as follows:
Case  $1$ : This position has at most  $4$  fancy pennies. If there are zero fancy stacks, the previous player has already won. Otherwise, there can only be one fancy stack, and it must have  $3$  pennies, contradicting the assumption that the position is fancy.
Case  $2$ : This position has  $5$  fancy pennies. Again, there can only be one fancy stack, and it must have  $5$  pennies. Then, the next player could split the stack into stacks of size  $1$  and  $4$ , after which the opponent wins by splitting the stack of size  $4$  into two stacks of size  $2$ . Otherwise, the next player would have to split the stack into stacks of size  $2$  and  $3$ , and then the opponent wins by splitting the stack of size  $3$  into stacks of size  $2$  and  $1$ .
Case  $3$ : This position has  $6$  fancy pennies. Then, there must be two fancy stacks, each with  $3$  pennies. The next player must split one of these stacks into stacks of size  $1$  and  $2$ , and then the opponent wins by splitting the other stack of size  $3$ .
Case  $4$ : This position has at least  $7$  fancy pennies. The next player must split a stack into two stacks, exactly one of which has an even number of pennies. Then, the opponent should split that stack into a stack of size  $1$  and another stack with an odd number of pennies. All the stacks will have an odd number of pennies again. In addition, the former player creates at most  $1$  stack of size  $1$  (since the other stack must have an even number of pennies), and the opponent creates either  $1$  or  $2$  stacks of size  $1$ . Thus, the number of fancy pennies decreases by at most  $3$ , so the new position has at least  $4$  fancy pennies remaining, so it must be fancy. In addition, the new position has fewer fancy pennies than the old position, which means that the next player must lose because we assumed that the old position is the minimal fancy position such that the next player can win.
In either case, we see that the next player must lose. Thus, by contradiction, there exists no fancy position such that the next player can win, as desired.
It immediately follows that the first player loses if  $n$  is odd and  $n > 3$ , since the initial position is fancy.
Finally, let us consider even  $n$ . If  $n = 4$ , the first player wins immediately by splitting the stack of size  $4$  into two stacks of size  $2$ . Otherwise, if  $n>4$ , the first player wins by splitting the stack into stacks of size  $1$  and  $n-1$ , creating a fancy position that causes the opponent to lose. $\therefore$  The first player wins if and only if  $n=3$  or  $n$  is even, as required.

By the way, I think that Luve96's solution contains an error, since Luve96's answer implies that the first player wins when  $n=7$ , but my solution shows that the first player loses instead.</details>
